title: What Buyers Should Know About the Preliminary Title Report
content_html:
Partway through escrow, most California buyers receive a document called a preliminary title report. It can run many pages, is full of unfamiliar abbreviations, and arrives at a point in the transaction when buyers are already juggling inspections, loan paperwork, and disclosures. It's easy to skim it and move on. That's a mistake — the preliminary title report is one of the most important documents you'll see before closing, because it tells you exactly what you're actually buying when you take title to a property.

What a Preliminary Title Report Actually Is

A preliminary title report is not an insurance policy, and it's not a guarantee of anything. It's an offer — a statement from a title company describing the condition of title to a specific property and the terms under which the company is willing to issue a title insurance policy once the sale closes. Think of it as a snapshot of the public record for that property: who currently holds title, and what liens, easements, restrictions, or other interests are recorded against it.

The report is typically ordered early in escrow, once the title company has a chance to search the chain of title and pull everything recorded against the parcel in the county records. For a Riverside County property, that means searching documents recorded with the Riverside County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder. The preliminary report is essentially a look backward at that recording history for the home you're buying.

Why It's Called "Preliminary"

The word "preliminary" matters. A preliminary report is a current snapshot, not a locked-in promise. Title can change between the date the report is issued and the date you actually close — a new lien could be recorded, a judgment could attach, or a document could surface that wasn't captured in the initial search. That's part of why title companies typically run an updated search close to closing, and why the final title insurance policy you receive after recording can differ slightly from the preliminary report you reviewed earlier in escrow. The preliminary report tells you what the title company sees today and what it would need resolved before insuring the sale.

What's Inside the Report

Preliminary title reports follow a fairly standard structure, even though the formatting varies between title companies. Here's what you'll typically find:

  • Vesting information. This shows how the current owner holds title — as a sole owner, with a spouse, in a trust, or through some other form of ownership. It confirms who is legally entitled to sell the property.
  • Legal description. The formal description of the property by lot, tract, and parcel — not just the street address.
  • Schedule A. The basic facts: the proposed insured, the type of policy to be issued, and the vesting and legal description just mentioned.
  • Schedule B, Exceptions. This is the section that deserves the closest reading. It lists everything the title company found recorded against the property that it is not automatically going to insure over — property taxes, easements, covenants, conditions and restrictions (CC&Rs), existing deeds of trust (mortgages) the seller hasn't paid off yet, liens, and any other recorded interests.
  • Requirements. Items that need to be cleared, paid off, or otherwise resolved before the title company will issue a final policy — most commonly, the seller's existing mortgage needs to be paid off and reconveyed at closing.

Reading the Exceptions Section Carefully

Most of what appears in Schedule B exceptions is routine and expected. Every property has some combination of recorded items that simply come with owning real estate and aren't cause for concern:

  • Property taxes for the current fiscal year, which are a standard lien against every parcel and get prorated between buyer and seller at closing.
  • CC&Rs and easements, especially in planned communities or HOAs, which govern things like architectural guidelines, shared maintenance responsibilities, or utility company access across part of the lot.
  • The seller's existing mortgage, which is expected to be paid off through escrow at closing and then formally released from the record.

What deserves a closer look — and a conversation with your real estate agent, escrow officer, or a real estate attorney — are items that aren't part of that routine list: an old lien from a contractor or a creditor, a judgment against a prior owner, a tax lien, an easement that seems to cut through the buildable part of the lot, or a restriction that conflicts with how you plan to use the property. None of these automatically kill a transaction. Most can be resolved before closing — paid off, released, or otherwise cleared — but someone needs to identify them and make sure they're handled, and that someone starts with you actually reading the report.

How the Report Connects to Title Insurance

The preliminary title report and your title insurance policy are closely related but not the same thing. The report is the title company's statement of what it found and what it's prepared to insure, subject to the listed exceptions. The policy is what you actually receive after closing, once those exceptions have been addressed or accepted. Exceptions that remain on the policy are, by definition, not covered by your title insurance — which is exactly why it matters to review them before you close rather than after.

What Buyers Should Actually Do With the Report

A few practical habits make a real difference here:

  • Read Schedule B in full, not just the summary your agent or escrow officer sends you. The exceptions section is where anything unusual will show up.
  • Ask questions about anything unfamiliar. Title company representatives, escrow officers, and your agent can usually explain what a given exception means and whether it's routine.
  • Pay attention to the legal description and vesting to make sure they match what you expect — the right parcel, and a seller who actually has authority to convey title.
  • Flag anything concerning early. The earlier an unexpected lien or dispute surfaces, the more time there is to resolve it before your closing date.
  • Keep a copy even after closing. If a title issue surfaces later, the preliminary report is a useful record of what was known and disclosed at the time of your purchase.

Buyers sometimes assume that because a title company is involved and title insurance is part of the deal, they don't need to personally review the preliminary report — that the professionals will catch anything important. In practice, the professionals are relying on you to flag anything that doesn't match your understanding of the property or your plans for it. An easement you didn't know about, a CC&R restriction that conflicts with a planned addition, or a lien tied to a name similar to the seller's are all things a careful read can catch early, while there's still time to work through them calmly rather than at the closing table.

A Normal Part of a California Purchase

None of this is meant to make the preliminary title report sound alarming. The overwhelming majority of these reports come back clean, with nothing more unusual than current-year property taxes and a CC&R package for the subdivision. The point isn't to expect a problem — it's to actually look, so that if something does need attention, it gets handled during escrow rather than discovered after you already own the property. Pairing a careful read of the preliminary report with the rest of your disclosure review gives you a fuller picture of exactly what you're buying before you commit to closing.
